strengths: The quadratic improvement on learning classical junta distributions (Theorem 1) from $O(2^{2k} k \log n / \epsilon^4)$ to $O(2^k k \log(n/\delta) / \epsilon^2)$ is tight and resolves the sample complexity by matching the lower bound of Aliakbarpour et al. (COLT 2016) in every parameter.

The definition and analysis of quantum junta states is natural and fills a clear gap in the quantum property testing and learning literature, providing nearly matching upper and lower bounds on copy complexity.

The observation that Choi states of $QAC^0$ circuits are close to juntas (Theorem 18) significantly improves the copy complexity of learning $QAC^0$ circuits from $n^{O((\log(s^2 2^a/\epsilon))^d)}$ to $2^{O((\log(s^2 2^a/\epsilon))^d)} \log n$, removing the polynomial base dependence on $n$.
The application of Theorem 18 yields improved circuit lower bounds for computing the address function with $QAC^0$ circuits.
The presentation is exceptionally lucid, cleanly organized, and provides self-contained, elegant proofs (including the Pauli-analytic derivation of classical shadow estimation guarantees).
weaknesses: The algorithmic runtimes for learning and testing junta distributions/states scale with $n^k$ because the algorithms exhaustively examine all $\binom{n}{k}$ coordinate subsets of size $k$; discussing whether sub-exhaustive variable identification can be achieved in certain regimes would add value.
Section 6 is conditional on an open problem in Fourier analysis (Question 24); while interesting and motivated by the Kindler-Safra theorem, it remains speculative without a full proof.

strengths: The paper resolves the sample complexity of learning classical junta distributions under total variation distance, improving the prior upper bound of O(2^{2k} k log(n) / eps^4) by Aliakbarpour et al. (COLT 2016) to O(2^k k log(n/delta) / eps^2), which matches the known lower bound in every parameter.

It naturally defines and initiates the study of quantum junta states, establishing nearly tight copy complexity bounds for learning them using simple, single-copy Pauli measurements via classical shadows, as well as characterizing their testing complexity.

It demonstrates that Choi states of QAC0 circuits are close to juntas (not merely concentrated on low degrees), which yields an exponential improvement in the qubit dimension n (reducing sample complexity from n^{polylog} to 2^{polylog} log(n)) for learning Choi states in normalized Frobenius norm.
The connection between QAC0 circuits and juntas is also fruitfully applied to prove improved lower bounds against QAC0 circuits computing the address function.
The paper is very well-written, clearly organized, and conceptually cohesive, tying together classical and quantum junta learning via Fourier and Pauli analytic perspectives.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic framework—refining the low-degree LMN algorithm via hard thresholding/sparsity—is conceptually straightforward and follows established paradigms in classical learning theory (e.g., Eskenazis et al., 2022), adapting them to the quantum Pauli setting.

For QAC0 circuits, in the standard regime where circuit size s = poly(n), the sample complexity bound remains quasipolynomial in n, so the exponential improvement in n primarily impacts the regime of small circuit sizes s.

Section 6 ('Towards better learning of AC0 circuits') relies on an unproven conjecture in Fourier analysis (Question 24), leaving the claimed improvement for AC0 learning and polynomial-size DNFs speculative.

There are minor mathematical typos and oversights: in Equation (22), the product has terms up to x_k a_k instead of x_D a_D for x in {-1, 1}^D; in Theorem 11, the sample complexity has a factor of k in the log term (log((3n)^k/delta) = k log(3n/delta)) which translates to an extra factor of k that was omitted or implicitly absorbed into the base in Theorem 3.

strengths: Resolves a natural open problem in classical distribution learning: improves the sample complexity of learning k-junta distributions from O(2^{2k} k log(n) / eps^4) (Aliakbarpour et al., COLT 2016) to O(2^k k log(n) / eps^2), matching their lower bound in every parameter.

Formulates a natural quantum analogue of junta distributions (quantum junta states) and establishes nearly matching upper and lower bounds for both learning (via single-copy Pauli measurements and classical shadows) and testing.

Substantially improves the sample/copy complexity for learning the Choi state of QAC0 circuits from n^{O((log(s^2 2^a/eps))^d)} to 2^{O((log(s^2 2^a/eps))^d)} log(n), which yields an exponential reduction in n for constant circuit size.
Derives a clean circuit lower bound against QAC0 for computing the address function, directly leveraging the fact that QAC0 circuits are close to juntas.
The paper is very well-written, with clear intuitions, precise proofs, and an elegant Pauli-analytic treatment of Classical Shadows.
weaknesses: The primary algorithmic technique—combining low-degree estimation with hard-thresholding rounding based on sparsity—is conceptually similar to prior work (e.g., Eskenazis, Ivanisvili, and Streck, 2022), although its adaptation across classical and quantum settings here is clean and effective.

The computational time complexity of the junta learning algorithms scales as O(n^k ...), requiring brute-force search over all low-degree coefficients or subsets of size k, so the computational efficiency is superpolynomial when k grows with n.

In the standard complexity regime where QAC0 circuit size s = poly(n), the sample complexity bound remains quasi-polynomial in n (2^{O(log^d n)}), which is the same qualitative regime as prior work by Nadimpalli et al.

Section 6 is conditioned on an open question in Fourier analysis (Question 24); while the connection and partial evidence via the Kindler-Safra theorem are interesting, the main conditional result remains unproven.

strengths: Optimal sample complexity for learning junta distributions: The paper resolves the sample complexity of learning k-junta distributions by improving the prior upper bound of Aliakbarpour et al. (COLT 2016) from O(2^{2k} k log(n) / eps^4) to O(2^k k log(n) / eps^2), matching the established information-theoretic lower bound in all parameters.

First study and near-optimal bounds for quantum junta states: The paper initiates the study of quantum junta states, providing an upper bound of O(12^k log(n) / eps^2) single-copy Pauli measurements using Classical Shadows and proving a matching-in-order lower bound of Omega((4^k + log(n)) / eps^2) via a clean Holevo information and subadditivity argument.

Stronger structural results and lower bounds for QAC^0 circuits: By recognizing that the Choi states of QAC^0 circuits are not just low-degree but actually close to juntas, the authors achieve an exponential improvement in the copy complexity of learning QAC^0 Choi states (in terms of circuit parameters) and obtain an improved circuit lower bound of s^2 2^a = Omega(2^{(2^D)^{1/d}}) for computing the D-address function.

Clear intuition and exposition: Section 1.5 provides a very transparent high-level explanation of why combining low-degree Fourier estimation with hard thresholding saves a factor of n^d in sample complexity.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty relies on known thresholding paradigms: The central algorithmic technique—estimating low-degree Fourier/Pauli coefficients followed by hard thresholding—is essentially an adaptation of the approach by Eskenazis, Ivanisvili, and Streck (2022) to the settings of probability distributions and quantum states.

Sample complexity vs. computational efficiency: While the sample and copy complexities are near-optimal, the running time of the algorithms scales with the number of degree-k monomials (i.e., Omega(n^k)), which is quasi-polynomial or exponential in k. The manuscript should more explicitly delineate sample complexity from time complexity.

Validity of estimated outputs: The estimators p'' and rho'' obtained after thresholding are not guaranteed to be a valid probability distribution (non-negative and summing to 1) or a valid quantum density operator (positive semidefinite with unit trace). While projecting onto the probability simplex or quantum state space in L2 / Frobenius norm is standard and non-expansive, this step should be explicitly stated and verified.

Typographical and notation inconsistencies in proofs: There are several minor slips that hinder reading, including: (1) In Section 1.5, Step 2 of the algorithm has confusing primes ('if |\hat{f}''(S)| \le ... set \hat{f}'(S) = 0, otherwise \hat{f}''(S) = \hat{f}'(S)'); (2) The numbering in Section 1.1 skips (iii); (3) At the top of page 15, the LHS of the display has \subseteq instead of \not\subseteq and writes \hat{\rho}_{\Phi'} instead of \hat{\rho}_{\Phi_\sigma}; (4) On page 12, the entropy bound nT S(\rho_{\varepsilon/n}) \le nT + TO(\varepsilon^2/n^2) has an unnecessary positive error term since S(\rho) \le 1.

strengths: Resolves a notable gap in classical distribution learning: The paper quadratically improves the sample complexity of learning k-junta distributions from O(2^(2k) k log(n) / eps^4) (Aliakbarpour et al., COLT 2016) to O(2^k k log(n/delta) / eps^2), significantly tightening the dependence on both k and epsilon.

First formulation and near-optimal bounds for quantum junta states: The manuscript naturally generalizes junta distributions to quantum junta states, achieving an upper bound of O(12^k k log(n/delta) / eps^2) single-copy Pauli measurements via classical shadow tomography and an almost matching lower bound of Omega((4^k + log n) / eps^2) via Holevo information and subadditivity.

Insightful structural observation for QAC0 circuits: The authors observe that the low-degree Pauli concentration proof of Nadimpalli et al. (STOC 2024) actually yields junta concentration for Choi states of n-to-1 QAC0 circuits, leading to an improved copy complexity dependence on n and double-exponentially stronger lower bounds for computing the address function.

Clean, transparent, and mathematically sound exposition: The proofs are concise, technically sound, and clearly articulate how the low-degree sparse rounding framework applies across classical and quantum domains.
weaknesses: Overstated optimality claims: The manuscript repeatedly claims that the junta distribution upper bound 'matches their lower bound in every parameter'. However, the lower bound of Aliakbarpour et al. is additive, Omega(2^k / eps^2 + k log(n) / eps), whereas the upper bound obtained here is multiplicative, O(2^k k log(n) / eps^2). While the epsilon and base-2^k scalings are improved, the dependence on n and k is not strictly matching.

Computational intractability: All presented algorithms require exhaustive enumeration over all subsets or Pauli observables of weight up to k, leading to an Omega(n^k) computational runtime. While the paper explicitly frames its contributions around sample and copy complexity, the lack of discussion regarding computational hardness and runtime trade-offs is a noticeable limitation for a machine learning venue.

Modest algorithmic novelty: The algorithmic primitive is largely an application of the hard-thresholding/rounding approach introduced by Eskenazis, Ivanisvili, and Streck (2022) for low-degree polynomials, paired with standard empirical Fourier estimation and classical shadow tomography.

Limited practical improvement for QAC0 in standard regimes: As the authors candidly note, in the canonical setting where circuit size s = poly(n) and depth d is constant, the sample complexity remains quasipolynomial (2^(log s)^d = n^(log n)^(d-1)), matching the qualitative complexity already established by Nadimpalli et al. (2023).

Minor presentation inconsistencies and omissions: The paper does not discuss projecting the thresholded estimator p'' back onto the probability simplex (p'' may have small negative entries or sum slightly differently from 1), and there are minor inconsistencies in the k factor between the summary in Table 1 and the formal theorem statements (e.g., Theorem 1 vs Table 1, and Theorem 8 vs Theorem 9).

strengths: The paper achieves an optimal sample complexity of $O(2^k k \log(n/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ for learning $k$-junta distributions under total variation distance, matching the lower bound of Aliakbarpour et al. (COLT 2016) in all parameters and quadratically improving the error dependence.

It initiates the study of learning quantum $k$-junta states, providing nearly matching upper and lower copy complexity bounds ($O(12^k \log(n/\delta)/\varepsilon^2)$ single copies via classical shadows vs. $\Omega((4^k + \log n)/\varepsilon^2)$). The Holevo-based lower bound argument establishing the $\Omega(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ term is concise and elegant.

The observation that the Pauli spectrum of QAC0 circuits is close to a junta (and not merely concentrated on low-degree) provides an exponential improvement in the $n$-dependence (from $n^{O((\log(s 2^a/\varepsilon))^d)}$ to $2^{O((\log(s 2^a/\varepsilon))^d)} \log n$) for learning the Choi state, as well as an improved circuit lower bound for the address function.

Section 1.5 offers clear and intuitive high-level motivation for why thresholding low-degree Fourier/Pauli estimates eliminates the blow-up caused by union-bounding over $\approx n^d$ coefficients when the underlying object is sparse/junta-supported.
weaknesses: There is an expository and technical gap in the proof of Corollary 14: the proof asserts that because the address function $f$ is far from Boolean juntas and the Choi state of the QAC0 circuit is close to a quantum junta state, the result follows. The author omits the necessary reduction showing that if a circuit computes $f$ with error $\le 1/4$, the diagonal of its channel/Choi state induces a real function bounded away from zero, which can then be rounded to a Boolean junta $g$ close to $f$.

In the proof of Theorem 10 (page 15), the summation indices in the first four display lines are erroneously written as $\sum_{\text{supp}(P) \subseteq [K']}$ and $\sum_{\text{supp}(P) \subset [K']}$ instead of the complementary tail $\sum_{\text{supp}(P) \not\subseteq K'}$.

In the Holevo information analysis on page 12, line 4 of the bound on $(*)$ states $\le nT + T O(\varepsilon^2/n^2)$. Multiplying $nT$ by $O((\varepsilon/n)^2)$ yields $O(T\varepsilon^2/n)$ rather than $T O(\varepsilon^2/n^2)$ (although this does not break the final $\chi \le O(T\varepsilon^2)$ bound).
In Equation (18) defining the $D$-address function, the product is written with an index running up to $k$ instead of $D$ ($x_k a_k$ instead of $x_D a_D$).

For Theorem 1, the output hypothesis $p''$ is an unnormalized polynomial which may take negative values or not sum to 1. While standard projection onto the probability simplex in $\ell_1$ norm resolves this without increasing error, this step should be explicitly stated.
